newsitem.title: USA: Condors released into wilds of Arizona.
newsitem.headline: Condors released into wilds of Arizona.

text.p: Six young California condors were released into the wilds of northern Arizona on Thursday in an effort to re-establish the endangered scavenger birds in the area.
It was the first time that the giant birds -- the largest and rarest in North America -- had been seen in the skies of the U.S. Southwest since 1924.

As about 400 onlookers watched from a mile (1.6 km) below, the six condors were sent off into the wild after being freed from holding pens on the 500-foot-high (152 metre) Vermilion Cliffs, about 115 miles (180 kms) north of Flagstaff.

Several of the fledglings, bred in captivity, hopped around and briefly took to the air in the rugged, isolated terrain near the Arizona-Utah border. Officials hope the condors will spread to the Grand Canyon and other areas.
The release, overseen by Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt, is part of an effort to re-establish the birds in the area and to ensure their survival.
Officials hope to establish a second independent population of condors in Arizona to go along with one in California, where there have been seven such releases.
"This is a magnificent symbol of how the Endangered Species Act can and does and is working," Babbitt said at a briefing last week on the Arizona release.
There currently are 121 California condors in the world, with 104 in captivity and 17 released to the wild in southern California.
The California condor, with a 10-foot (3-metre) wingspan and weighing more than 20 pounds (9 kgs), is the largest land bird in North America and once flew over vast stretches of the West.
Its population had declined to just 21 birds, but was brought back from the brink of extinction with captive breeding programmes.
Arizona offers wilder land with less human interference than southern California, and the Interior Department hopes to release more birds there on a yearly basis.
Babbitt said the condors will have minimal effect on how the land in the northern Arizona region can be used, and will not impede hunting, grazing livestock or other activities.
